deep.reconstruction:
Problem (Aufgabe): a light ray meets a refracting sphere of radius r centred at the origin. The refractive ratio is n:1, with the ray passing from the rarer medium (index 1) into the denser (index n) and travelling in the +x direction. The incident ray is y = α + μx, z = β + νx and the refracted ray is y = α' + μ'x, z = β' + ν'x. The task is to find α', β', μ', ν' from α, β, μ, ν. Gauss does not give the general 3D answer. He treats two special cases; together with the rotational symmetry about any line through the centre, these contain the whole solution, because the refracted ray stays in the plane through the centre and the incident ray.

Case 1 (μ = ν = 0, ray parallel to the axis at distance ρ, ρ² = α² + β²).
- Write A = n²r² − ρ² and B = r² − ρ² (notation mine).
- The ray hits the sphere at x0 = −√B, with sin i = ρ/r. Snell's law gives sin i' = ρ/(nr).
- The deviation δ = i − i' satisfies sin δ = ρ(√A − √B)/(nr²) (step mine).
- The refracted line keeps distance r sin i' = ρ/n from the centre, so it meets the axis at X = (ρ/n)/sin δ = r²/(√A − √B) = (√A + √B)/(n² − 1). This is Gauss's formula; for ρ → 0 it gives r/(n−1), the paraxial focus of a single surface.
- The refracted ray joins (−√B, ρ) to (X, 0). By similar triangles, its height at x = 0 is α' = α·X/(X + √B), and X + √B = (√A + n²√B)/(n² − 1). Hence α' = α(√A + √B)/(√A + n²√B) and μ' = −α/(X + √B) = −α(n² − 1)/(√A + n²√B). The same factors apply to β' and ν'.

Case 2 (β = ν = 0, meridional ray in the xy-plane with arbitrary slope).
- Put P = √((1+μ²)r² − α²), Q = √((1+μ²)n²r² − α²) and N = n²P + Q + αμ(n² − 1).
- Intersecting y = α + μx with x² + y² = r² gives the point of incidence x0 = (−αμ − P)/(1 + μ²) (step mine).
- Gauss states α' = α(P + Q)/N. The equivalent form α − α(n²−1)(P + αμ)/N follows by direct expansion.
- He also states μ' = μ − α(1 + μ²)(n² − 1)/N.

Normalisation by the distance from the centre.
- Put α = λ√(1+μ²) and α' = λ'√(1+μ'²), so that λ and λ' are the perpendicular distances of the incident and refracted lines from the centre.
- Gauss obtains λ' = λ/n. This is Snell's law written as r sin i = n·r sin i'.
- Dividing N by √(1+μ²) gives μ' = μ − λ(1 + μ²)(n² − 1)/(n²√(r² − λ²) + √(n²r² − λ²) + (n² − 1)λμ).

Why this holds (verification mine): the refracted direction is θ' = θ − δ, with tan θ = μ and δ = i − i', sin i = λ/r, sin i' = λ/(nr). Then μ − μ' = (1 + μ²)/(cot δ + μ). A short computation gives cot δ = (√(n²r²−λ²)·√(r²−λ²) + λ²)/(λ(√(n²r²−λ²) − √(r²−λ²))) = (n²√(r²−λ²) + √(n²r²−λ²))/((n²−1)λ), which reproduces Gauss's formula exactly.

Purpose: this is exact (non-paraxial) ray tracing through one spherical refracting surface, written in line coordinates. The next page (f.91) continues with the image of a point, in angle form and in the paraxial limit, i.e. groundwork for Gauss's dioptrics.
errors: No mathematical errors found; all formulas check out symbolically and numerically (e.g. r=1, n=2, μ=0, α=0.5 gives α'=0.25946, μ'=−0.27775, λ'=0.25=λ/n, and the refracted line passes through the point of incidence).
Notational slip: the refracted-ray equation is written 'z' = β' + ν'x'; it should be z = β' + ν'x, since the primes belong on the parameters, not the coordinate.

Implicit conventions not stated: light travels in +x, enters the denser medium (index n) at the near intersection x0 = −√(r²−ρ²), and all square roots are positive. The λ-form also assumes positive √(1+μ'²). These are consistent with the results but unstated.
The general case (μ, ν, β all nonzero) announced in the problem is not worked out on this page; only the two special cases are given. They suffice by rotational symmetry, but this is not said.

results.what: Exact axis-crossing point of a refracted ray parallel to the axis at height ρ: x = (√(n²r²−ρ²) + √(r²−ρ²))/(n²−1) from the centre, with intercept and slope of the refracted ray
results.modern_name: Exact (non-paraxial) ray trace through a spherical refracting surface; longitudinal spherical aberration of a single surface
results.usually_credited_to: Classical: Descartes, Huygens (Traité de la lumière / Dioptrica, 17th c.)

results.what: Invariant λ' = λ/n: the perpendicular distance of the ray from the sphere's centre is divided by n on refraction
results.modern_name: Snell's law in the form n·r·sin i = const (ray invariant for spherical symmetry; Bouguer's formula)
results.usually_credited_to: Bouguer (1729) for atmospheric refraction; standard in geometric optics

results.what: Closed formulas for intercept and slope of a refracted meridional ray: α' = α(P+Q)/N and μ' = μ − α(1+μ²)(n²−1)/N, plus the λ-normalised form
results.modern_name: Meridional exact ray-tracing formulas in line (intercept–slope) coordinates
results.usually_credited_to: Exact trigonometric ray tracing is standard 18th–19th c. optics (Euler, Klügel, later Seidel); this specific algebraic form is not attributed to anyone

deep.surprise_reason: This is correct but elementary exact ray tracing through one spherical surface; the λ'=λ/n invariant is just Snell's law. It is a preliminary to Gauss's known dioptric work (Dioptrische Untersuchungen, 1841), and his interest in optics around 1809 onward is well documented. The neat line-coordinate formulation is a pleasant detail, not new mathematics.

transcription_corrections: The line written 'z' = β' + ν'x' is transcribed faithfully; the prime on z is Gauss's own slip and should be z.
The margin shelf-mark at top left reads approximately 'XI 1, §131' (archival annotation); it is not in the machine transcription.
Otherwise the transcription matches the image: P, Q, N 'gesetzt', and the final λ-form of μ' with the denominator nn√(rr−λλ) + √(nnrr−λλ) + (nn−1)λμ.
